fossil
The papersThe code

Random forests in linkage disequilibrium, dug back up.

34 results: 11 exact, 7 agree, 10 partly agree, 1 differs, 5 not attempted. The lost program was rebuilt from the paper and checked against Breiman and Cutler's Fortran, and the simulations were run again.

See every result

One of 50 points misses: the paper's curve at X = 12 (0.44) is read where ours jumps from 0.23 at X = 12 to 0.81 at X = 13; half a step of X, about one pixel, covers it. One of 45 points misses: RF0:IM1 with 1 LD.rSNP at X = 5 reads 0.13 where our curve goes 0.00, 0.06, 0.80 at X = 5, 6, 7; at X = 5.5 it is 0.03, within tolerance.

Fig. 4

Fig. 4. Mean IM of the risk SNPs, true risk haplotypes and predicted risk haplotypes (H4M4, K4S4N100) against r² between the two SNPs of a risk haplotype.

Partly agrees
Fig. 4, mean IM of risk SNPs, true and predicted risk haplotypes (33 bars)
30 of 33 values, Partly agrees

30 of 33 bars agree. The paper's PRED.rHAP bars are all the same height (0.654, error bars too): two of them miss ours at r2 = 0 and 0.1, a plotting slip. The rHAP bar at r2 = 0 (0.565 against our 0.736) is the low-r2 gap of Fig. 5.

Fig. 5

Fig. 5. Share of replicates where every risk SNP, risk haplotype or predicted haplotype has a higher IM than every noise SNP.

Partly agrees
Fig. 5, share of replicates with all risk variables above the noise (33 bars)
28 of 33 values, Partly agrees

At r2 0-0.4 the paper's true haplotypes beat every noise SNP in 40-45% of replicates, ours in 72-76%; from r2 = 0.5 on they agree. Our risk haplotypes carry the same risk at every r2, as the model says, so ours stay flat.

Fig. 6

Fig. 6. Share of replicates with all risk variables among the top X: (a) SNPs, both and the best SNP of each haplotype; (b) true and predicted haplotypes; (c) the four codings at r² = 0 and 0.9.

Partly agrees
Fig. 6a, top X curves of the risk SNPs (both, and the best of each pair)
25 of 26 values, Partly agrees
Fig. 6b, top X curves of true and predicted haplotypes
14 of 27 values, Partly agrees
Fig. 6c, the four codings at r2 = 0 and 0.9
8 of 18 values, Partly agrees

One of 26 points misses: at X = 5 the best-SNP curve for r2 = 1 reads 0.12, but with r2 = 1 the two SNPs are copies and ours is 0; our r2 = 0.9 curve (dark red, next to red in the 87 dpi figure) is 0.21 there. The paper's true and predicted haplotype curves are low at small r2; ours are high at every r2. At r2 = 0 the published curve also contradicts the paper's own Fig. 5: 40% of replicates have all four risk haplotypes above every noise SNP, so at least 40% have them in the top 5, but the curve reads 12%. At r2 = 0 the paper's HAP and PRED.HAP curves are low and ours high (the low-r2 gap of Figs 5 and 6b); the SNP and best-SNP curves agree except one best-SNP point. At r2 = 0.9 all four codings agree.

Every result

Every figure, table and claim of the paper. A figure value agrees when it is within 3 combined Monte Carlo standard errors and one pixel of the published one.

The main claim holds for the paper's H4M4 figures and five of the six other models: the revised importance with the original forest is the steadiest under LD. It does not hold for H1M1 (open). Fig. 2's swapped series and Fig. 4's repeated bars are slips in the paper; the low-r2 haplotype gap of Figs 4 to 6 is open.

What came back

Table 1
Every K, lambda_s and GRR from the model parameters; one GRR is a rounding slip.
Fig. 1
All 40 mean importances within Monte Carlo error.
Fig. 2
All 40 bars, once two swapped series are put back.
Fig. 3
120 of 122 curve points; the two misses sit on vertical jumps.
The program
Random Forests 5.1 with RF1 and IM1, as the Python package rfld, checked against the Fortran original.

What stayed buried

  • Tables 2 to 4: the TGen Alzheimer genotypes were only ever handed out by request.
  • The threshold R of the revised forest is not in the paper; any R from 0.1 to just below 1 gives the same result here.
  • Why the paper's true haplotypes do worse at low r2 than the model gives (Figs 4 to 6): three candidate causes ruled out.

The main claim holds for the paper's H4M4 figures and five of the six other models: the revised importance with the original forest is the steadiest under LD. It does not hold for H1M1 (open). Fig. 2's swapped series and Fig. 4's repeated bars are slips in the paper; the low-r2 haplotype gap of Figs 4 to 6 is open.

What we matched

How each part of the paper's method was rebuilt.

Forest
A step-by-step port of Random Forests 5.1 for categorical SNPs, 5000 trees, mtry 35.
RF1
A tree drops every SNP with r2 above R with a SNP it already uses.
IM1
The permutation importance over the trees that use the SNP.
Data
Lunetta et al.'s heterogeneity-multiplicative models; 100 replicates of 250 cases and 250 controls.
Haplotypes
EM phasing as in haplo.stats, 100 sampled phasings with 1000 trees each.

Random forests in LD came back from the paper's text, with one program still online to check against.
